# Notes on Judges 11

**What I found:** Teachers in the same tradition disagree with each other, especially on vv. 30–31 and 39. So I've grouped the views by argument, not by denomination, and noted each teacher's tradition where it's clear.

**Gaps:**
- I found nothing on Judges 11 from the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), the Orthodox site (oca.org), or Pentecostal-specific sites (ag.org, pneumareview.com, samstorms.org). Those traditions are left out.
- I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
- I couldn't read Gill or Ellicott in full; the Enduring Word page was cut off after v. 33; and the NET notes I read stop partway through the chapter.
- Pages I read in full don't allow sentence-level citations, so for those I've just given the URL after each point.

---

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says Jephthah was brave but came from a shameful family background. He notes that "Gilead" is both the region east of the Jordan and, by coincidence, the name of Jephthah's father. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
- Guzik also quotes Morgan: God did not treat a wrong Jephthah wasn't responsible for as a reason to disqualify him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
- Adam Clarke (Methodist) thinks the Hebrew word translated "harlot" should be read as "hostess," meaning an innkeeper. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-11.html
- The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary says she may have been a concubine or a foreigner. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/judges-11.html
- Constable says the name Jephthah means "He [God] has opened [the womb]." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-11.html
- *Modern scholarship (Barnes):* The Jephthah story may have been a separate account added by whoever compiled Judges. Barnes doubts Gilead was literally Jephthah's father, since Gilead was Manasseh's grandson; "Gilead" may mean the head of the clan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html

**v. 2**
- JFB: Since there were sons by the lawful wife, a son by a second woman had no right to the inheritance. The brothers' rough treatment, though, suggests they also disliked him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/judges-11.html
- Wesley disagrees: being driven out cost Jephthah a share of his father's goods that was rightly his, even as an illegitimate son. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/judges/11.htm

**v. 3**
- Clarke: the "worthless men" may simply have been poor men without land or work. Guzik quotes Wood: Jephthah's band may have worked like David's men, guarding towns from raiders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
- Wesley: these men preferred to live by plunder. But Jephthah handled them well, turning them against Israel's enemies, especially Ammonite raiding parties. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/judges/11.htm
- JFB compares Jephthah's life here to David's after he fled from Saul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/judges-11.html
- Barnes places Tob north of Gilead, toward Damascus, and suggests it was his mother's homeland. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html

**vv. 4–5**
- Wesley says the elders went to Jephthah "by direction from God," and might not otherwise have chosen an illegitimate son. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/judges/11.htm
- JFB: the writer, having introduced Jephthah, now picks the story back up from 10:17. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/judges-11.html
- *Contrasting view:* An ESV Study Bible note quoted by Precept Austin says that, unlike earlier judges, Jephthah was not "raised up" by God. The people chose him without seeking God's approval, which the note treats as another sign of their drift from God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_11_commentary

**vv. 6–8**
- Guzik quotes Trapp's application of v. 7: we too rarely look for God until we have to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
- NET note: the elders first offer only "commander" (*qatsin*). When Jephthah resists, they raise the offer to "head" (*ro'sh*), meaning ruler of the region. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=11

**vv. 9–10**
- Guzik: Jephthah would only lead in the crisis if he stayed leader afterwards; he didn't want to be rejected again. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
- Barnes is more critical: Jephthah made his own rise in status the condition for saving his country, yet he is still listed among the faithful in Hebrews 11:32. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html
- Wesley on v. 10: the Hebrew literally says "The LORD be a hearer," a reminder that God hears whatever we say. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/judges/11.htm
- NET note: v. 9 is better read as a statement than a question. Jephthah is formally stating the terms, and in v. 10 the elders bind themselves to them by oath. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=11

**v. 11**
- Guzik links Mizpah ("watchtower") to Jacob and Laban's agreement in Genesis 31: God sees if a promise is broken. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
- Clarke: the elders' choice needed the people's confirmation, which is why "the people" made him head. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-11.html
- Barnes: "before the LORD" points to the presence of the tabernacle, the ark, or the high priest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html
- A sermon outline on Precept Austin teaches that the Spirit came on Jephthah only after he had yielded to the Lord here. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_commentaries
- NET note gives an alternative reading: "conducted business before the Lord," meaning he ruled under God's authority. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=11

**vv. 12–13**
- Wesley: Jephthah sent envoys to avoid bloodshed, showing "great prudence, and no less piety." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/judges/11.htm
- Clarke: he wanted the Ammonites to state their reasons so the justice of Israel's cause would be clearer to the people. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-11.html
- Barnes: the land Ammon claimed had once been Sihon's kingdom and then belonged to Reuben and Gad. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html

**vv. 14–22**
- Guzik: Jephthah's point is that Israel took the land from the Amorites, who had earlier taken it from Ammon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
- Barnes: Jephthah's account closely matches Numbers and Deuteronomy, which may mean a copy of the Law was at Mizpah. Barnes adds that the Pentateuch never mentions the embassy to Moab in v. 17. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html
- Precept Austin: Jephthah stands firmly on God's word and is trying to save lives. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_11_commentary

**vv. 23–24**
- Guzik: Jephthah sees this first as a contest between the LORD and Chemosh, a spiritual battle. Chemosh was really Moab's god, but the two nations may have shared gods. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
- NET note:
  - Treating Chemosh as if he were on a level with the LORD doesn't necessarily make Jephthah a polytheist; he may just be arguing from the king's point of view.
  - Ammon had probably conquered Moab and taken over its claims to the land.
- Barnes agrees the disputed land had been Moab's, which explains the mention of Chemosh. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html

**vv. 25–26**
- NET note: Balak tried to curse Israel, failed, and went home without fighting. The Ammonite king should follow his example. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=11
- Guzik quotes Cundall: the "three hundred years" is very close to the total of the time spans given in Judges so far (319 years). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/

**vv. 27–28**
- Wesley: Jephthah lets God settle the dispute by how the war turns out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/judges/11.htm
- Guzik: the king ignored a reasoned argument, so war could not be avoided. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/

**v. 29**
- **Agreed:** the Spirit's coming means God equipped Jephthah for the task.
  - Clarke: God thereby gave Jephthah the clearest proof that his cause was good. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-11.html
  - Coffman: this placed Jephthah among Israel's great Spirit-led leaders. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/11-29.html
- **Debated: does the Spirit's coming approve what Jephthah did next?**
  - Ellicott: it gave him the power for the deliverance "and that only," with no approval of his later actions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/11-29.htm
  - Barnes: the Spirit gave him courage and strength for battle, not spiritual wisdom, just as Gideon still went wrong over the ephod. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel, the nearest to a charismatic voice I found) applies this to believers: be filled with the Spirit to overcome fear. He adds that even a Spirit-filled man can act foolishly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
  - Miles Van Pelt (Reformed, The Gospel Coalition) argues the opposite: since the vow follows the Spirit's coming, it came under the Spirit's influence rather than against it. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/rethinking-jephthah-foolish-vow/
- *Modern scholarship:* The Cambridge Bible suggests the verse was an editor's link added after a long inserted section (vv. 12–28). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/11-29.htm

**vv. 30–31 — the vow (the biggest dividing point)**
- **Common ground:** almost every source calls the vow rash or foolish.
  - Guzik: such vows can be attempts to manipulate God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
  - Constable quotes Phyllis Trible: the vow showed doubt, not faith; it was an attempt to control God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/11-29.html
- **Reading A: he was thinking of an animal, or the vow allows two outcomes.**
  - Guzik, drawing on Clarke, renders it "shall be the LORD's, *or* I will offer it." A person would be dedicated to God; an animal would be burned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
  - A Bible Hub article makes the same grammar argument. https://biblehub.com/q/Did_Jephthah_sacrifice_his_daughter.htm
  - Clarke (Methodist): the Spirit would not have let Jephthah shed his child's blood. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-11.html
- **Reading B: he had a person in mind.**
  - Barnes (Presbyterian): only a member of the household would come out of the door to meet him, so he meant a human sacrifice. Barnes links this to his Syrian surroundings, where such sacrifices were probably common. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html
  - NET note:
    - The wording can include people.
    - He probably intended a human offering from the start.
    - He did not expect his daughter to be first. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=11
  - Catholic Answers holds the middle view: houses kept animals on the ground floor, so Jephthah likely expected a goat. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-two-foolish-mistakes-of-jephthah

**vv. 32–33**
- Guzik: God won a great victory through a man with a hard past. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
- Wesley: Jephthah did not try to take the Ammonites' land; others wronging us doesn't give us the right to wrong them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/judges/11.htm
- Barnes: it was a defensive battle fought on Israel's own land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html

**v. 34**
- Barnes: "only child" is the same word used of Isaac in Genesis 22. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html
- The Bible Hub study notes link the tambourines and dancing to Miriam's celebration in Exodus 15. https://biblehub.com/judges/11-34.htm

**v. 35**
- Constable points out a wordplay: "given my word" is literally "opened my mouth," and Jephthah's name means "he opens." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-11.html
- **Should he have kept the vow?**
  - Guzik: no. He should have repented and broken it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
  - Ligonier (Reformed) agrees. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jephthahs-rash-vow
  - Barnes: he was right not to let personal grief stop him keeping a vow, but wrong in the picture of God behind it, and would have done right not to kill her. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html

**v. 36**
- Barnes: her calm acceptance shows how deeply pagan ideas about human sacrifice had taken root. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html
- Older sermons on Bible Hub praise her obedience; one (Ritchie) sees in it a picture of Christ keeping his vow at the cross. https://biblehub.com/sermons/judges/11-34.htm
- Van Pelt: her willing agreement fits badly with a literal killing. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/rethinking-jephthah-foolish-vow/

**vv. 37–38**
- **For lifelong virginity:**
  - The text's concern is always her virginity, never her death. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/rethinking-jephthah-foolish-vow/
  - Got Questions notes she mourns never marrying rather than dying. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jephthahs-daughter.html
- **For a literal sacrifice:**
  - Barnes: becoming a wife and mother was an Israelite girl's great hope, and an early death would take that away. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html
  - Bible Hub's sermon collection: why ask for two months to mourn if she had decades ahead of her? https://biblehub.com/sermons/judges/11-34.htm

**v. 39 — what did he actually do?**
- **She was dedicated, not killed.**
  - Wesley (Methodist) says plainly she was "only devoted to perpetual virginity." He is astonished most commentators assume Jephthah murdered her. He argues that if Jephthah would not have burned a forbidden animal, he would not have committed forbidden murder. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/judges/11.htm
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel) points to Leviticus 27 (people vowed to God could be redeemed) and to the women who served at the tabernacle door. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
  - Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary leans this way, while admitting it is hard to know. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/11-29.htm
  - Van Pelt (Reformed, The Gospel Coalition) argues for dedication too. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/rethinking-jephthah-foolish-vow/
- **She was sacrificed.**
  - Ligonier (Reformed): ancient commentators held she was killed, and nothing in the language suggests otherwise. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jephthahs-rash-vow
  - Bible.org (Deffinbaugh): God was no more pleased than with Samson's immorality; Jephthah kept the vow to save face. https://bible.org/question/why-did-god-accept-and-allow-jepthath%E2%80%99s-sacrifice-his-daughter-judges-1129
  - Barnes takes the same view. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html
- **Undecided:** Got Questions sees signs both ways, but says "he did to her as he had vowed" points to the sacrifice. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jephthahs-daughter.html
- *Modern scholarship:*
  - NET note: the Hebrew grammar of "she had never known a man" more likely describes her state when the vow was carried out, not a life of celibacy. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=11
  - Bible Odyssey states flatly that Jephthah sacrificed his daughter. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/jephthah/
- *Catholic:*
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia says the plain sense is a human sacrifice, the "unanimous interpretation" of Jewish and early Christian tradition. It treats the virginity view as a modern attempt to defend Jephthah. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08333b.htm
  - Elsewhere it blames pagan influence, not the true worship of God. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/13309a.htm?highlight=WyJPdGhvIEZyZW5jaCBTdHJhaGwiXQ%3D%3D
  - Augustine asks whether Jephthah killed her at God's command. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120101.htm
  - Catholic Answers: his mistake was doubled; he made a foolish vow, then carried it out instead of repenting. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-two-foolish-mistakes-of-jephthah
- *Eastern Christian (Syriac):* Aphrahat, an early church father, says Jephthah sacrificed his daughter and draws parallels with Christ: driven out by his brothers, then made leader. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/370121.htm

**v. 40**
- Barnes: this yearly mourning is mentioned nowhere else, and the poetic style suggests it comes from an ancient song. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/judges-11.html
- The Bible Hub article supporting dedication argues four days of remembrance looks more like festival visits than funeral mourning. https://biblehub.com/q/Did_Jephthah_sacrifice_his_daughter.htm

**Linked to Hebrews 11:32 (affects vv. 1, 29, 39)**
- Several defenders of the virginity view say Jephthah's place among the faithful in Hebrews 11 is their key reason. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-11/
- Ligonier replies that this difficulty is the likely reason people avoid the sacrifice reading. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jephthahs-rash-vow
- Ellicott: Hebrews praises only Jephthah's faith at key moments, not his character overall. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/11-29.htm
